In the input, you should see... the blue grid only.

The output grid size...same as the input grid. copy the input grid.

To make the output, you have to...draw a down line with yellow to which the red grid's row meet. and continue the yellow grid to the side of the red grid

content.text:
Let me understand the rule via the verifier.

Input: grid with background 0, an 8 cell (x0) and a 2 cell (x1).

x2 = first(x0) = 8's location. x3 = first(x1) = 2's location.
x4 = last(x2) — for a single-cell frozenset, last(x2) = max(enumerate(x2))[1] = the only element. So x4 = x2 = 8 location.

Hmm wait, x0 = ofcolor(I, EIGHT) is a set of indices. first(x0) = the 8 position. last(x2) — x2 is a tuple (i,j), last of a tuple = max(enumerate(x2))[1]. For (i,j), enumerate gives (0,i),(1,j), max picks the larger value... Actually max(enumerate(x2)) compares tuples (0,i) vs (1,j), so second tuple wins => returns j. So x4 = j coordinate of 8! Interesting.

x5 = first(x3) = i coordinate of 2.
x6 = astuple(x5, x4) = (row of 2, col of 8).

Then x7 = connect(x6, x2) where x2 = (row8, col8). Both are... x6 = (row2, col8), x2 = (row8, col8). Same column! So connect gives vertical line from min row to max row at col8. That's the yellow (4) down line at the 8's column, from row of 2 to row of 8.

x8 = connect(x6, x3) where x3 = (row2, col2). Same row! So horizontal line from col8 to col2 at row2. That's the horizontal line.

x9 = union. x10 = underfill(I, FOUR, x9) — fill 4 only where background.

So output: horizontal yellow line at 2's row from 8's column to 2's column, and vertical yellow line at 8's column from 2's row to 8's row. The 2 remains red at its cell, 8 remains at its cell.

Check with example: 2 at row5, col6. 8 at row9, col4. x6 = (5, 4). x7 connect((5,4),(9,4)) vertical from row5 to row9 at col4: (5,4),(6,4),(7,4),(8,4),(9,4). But (9,4) is the 8 — underfill won't change it. x8 connect((5,4),(5,6)) horizontal at row5: (5,4),(5,5),(5,6). (5,6) is the 2 - underfill won't change. Output shows row5: col4,5 = 4, col6=2; col4 down rows 5-9 yes. Matches.

So I need to teach this. Now the exam uses held-out generator inputs. The dimensions/sizes may vary. The key rule: draw 4 along the vertical line at 8's column between 8's row and 2's row, and horizontal line at 2's row between the columns, filling only background.

Since x6 uses row of 2 and col of 8, effectively corner point. Let me just teach with a clear example.

Let me create a demonstration with different positions to be clear. Actually better to show multiple demonstrations with varied positions. Let's make a couple of show_transformed_input calls (environment fills gold), which is most reliable — no risk of mismatch.

Let me do one: place 8 and 2 in different spots.

Let me be careful: the "corner" is at (row of 2, col of 8). Lines: vertical at col8 from row2 to row8, horizontal at row2 from col2 to col8.

Let me author a few examples to help student generalize.

Example A: 8 at row2 col7, 2 at row6 col1 in a 9x9 grid.
Vertical: col7 rows2..6 -> 4. Horizontal: row6? wait horizontal at row of 2 = row6, from col1 to col7. Hmm recompute: vertical at col of 8 (7), from row of 2 (6) to row of 8 (2). Horizontal at row of 2 (6) from col2 (1) to col8 (7). So corner at (6,7).

Let me just use show_transformed_input so environment computes gold. Then verify by querying? Actually show_transformed_input shows the pair to student directly. Good.

Let me provide a few varied demonstrations. I'll do 2-3.

Then maybe a query_student to check understanding, but query uses my authored input and student predicts; gold given. But I need to author input correctly following conventions. Fine.

Let me do show_transformed_input twice with different arrangements, then start exam.

Example 1: grid 11x11, 8 at (3,8), 2 at (9,2).
Vertical: col8, rows3..9. Horizontal: row9, cols2..8. Corner (9,8).

Example 2: grid 8x12, 8 at (6,10), 2 at (1,3).
Vertical: col10 rows1..6. Horizontal: row1 cols3..10.

I'll just send inputs.

Let me construct Example 1 grid 11x11 all zeros, 8 at row3 col8, 2 at row9 col2.

Example 2: grid 8 rows x 12 cols, 8 at row6 col10, 2 at row1 col3.

These give clear teaching. Also maybe a third where 8 is above/right of 2, to show general arrangement.

Example 3: 8 at (10,1)? Wait must have both. Let's do 8 at (8,9), 2 at (2,5): vertical col9 rows2..8, horizontal row2 cols5..9.

I'll do all three, then start_exam.

Let me write them.

tools.name: show_example

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

output_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Show the Student a labeled input-output pair that you authored. If your output matches the rule, the pair is shown and you receive a success acknowledgement only. If it does not match, the pair is not shown and you receive the gold output so you can correct it.

tools.name: show_transformed_input

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Provide only an input grid. The environment applies the verifier and shows the resulting gold input-output pair to the student.

tools.name: query_student

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Probe the student with an input of your choice. You receive the student's predicted output, the gold output, and whether they matched. The student does not see the gold pair unless you later show it with show_example or show_transformed_input.

tools.name: start_exam
tools.description: End teaching and send the student to the exam: they must solve held-out generator inputs (unseen in demonstrations or probes) with the history so far. No further teaching after this.

content.text:
Three demonstrations shown. Let me do a probe to verify student understanding, then start exam.

Probe: 8 at (1,9), 2 at (7,4) in a grid. Vertical col9 rows1..7, horizontal row7 cols4..9.

Grid 9x11.

Let me send query.
